the-analyst-workflow.title: Welcome to The data analyst's workflow, part of Data Science & Analytics.
the-analyst-workflow.idea: Most "data projects" that fail do not fail at the algorithm. They fail at the question (nobody agreed what was being decided), the data (the numbers did not mean what the column name suggested), or the handover (a correct answer nobody trusted or acted on). Learning the workflow is therefore not administration; it is the part of the job that determines whether the work matters.
the-analyst-workflow.example: The request arrives as: "Management says attendance is bad. Can you look at the data?" The first job is to refuse to answer it, politely, and ask instead: which attendance, over what period, compared with what, and what decision is pending? Three clarifying messages later the question is: "Of the 1,240 students enrolled in the IT Essentials program between January and June 2026, what proportion attended at least 70% of scheduled sessions each month, and did that proportion change between the two terms?" Now the work is defined. The population is named (1,240 enrolled students), the metric is unambiguous (proportion attending ≥ 70% of sessions per month), the comparison is set (term 1 versus term 2), and a plausible answer — whether attendance improved or worsened — would change what the school does next, which is the test of whether the question was worth asking. The extraction is a single query over two tables, grouped by month; the cleaning stage discovers that 43 students were counted twice because they re-registered after the subsidy scheme, and that Term 2 has a public-holiday week with no sessions in it. Both are corrected and both are written in the notes, because the honest version of the answer depends on them.
the-analyst-workflow.challenge: Choose a real decision facing an organisation you know and build the complete framing document: the question, the population, the metric and its exact definition, the period, the data sources with their owners, the two most likely biases in that data, and the decision rule — what result would lead to which action. No analysis yet. Have it reviewed by somebody who will use the answer, and revise it until they agree it is the right question.

cleaning-and-preparing-data.title: Welcome to Cleaning and preparing data, part of Data Science & Analytics.
cleaning-and-preparing-data.idea: The moment a dataset arrives from the real world — a school register, a shop's sales export, a mobile-money statement — it stops being abstract and becomes a set of specific annoyances: Kofi Mensah and KOFI MENSAH , phone numbers that Excel has turned into 2.33E+09, blank cells where a fee was waived, and one transaction for GH₵9,999,999 that turns out to be a test entry. Cleaning is where analysis is either saved or ruined.
cleaning-and-preparing-data.example: The file has 1,247 rows, 9 columns, and the problems every real export has. The profile output below is the first thing to generate, because it turns "this file is a mess" into a list of specific tasks. Reading it: studentid is fine (1,240 distinct values, so seven duplicates to investigate). feepaid is text for 312 rows because somebody typed N/A and a currency symbol, which means any sum of that column is either wrong or refusing to compute. dob has impossible dates (year 1016, and one 2199) — typos, not data. enrolled_at is missing for 18 rows and all 18 come from one intake day, which suggests a batch upload failure rather than random loss — so the missingness is MAR at best and should be reported. gender has seven spellings of two values. The repair is a script rather than a series of manual edits, so it can be re-run when the next export arrives: this month's fixes become next month's automated step.
cleaning-and-preparing-data.challenge: Take the messiest dataset you can obtain — ideally one from a real organisation with duplicates, blanks and inconsistent categories — and produce a cleaning script plus a one-page data quality report: what was wrong, what you did, what you could not fix, what the total reconciles against, and the three remaining limitations somebody using this data must know. Then hand it to a colleague and ask them to re-run it from scratch on a fresh export.

describing-and-visualising-data.title: Welcome to Describing and visualising data, part of Data Science & Analytics.
describing-and-visualising-data.idea: Two analyses of the same school can reach opposite conclusions while both being arithmetically correct, simply by choosing an average or a chart that hides the shape of the data. The skill in this lesson is not decorative: it is being able to describe a distribution in four numbers and one picture, so that whoever reads it can make a decision without being misled — and so that if you are misleading them, you can tell.
describing-and-visualising-data.example: A Ghanaian training centre has 412 fee payments recorded in a term. The mean is GH₵742, the median GH₵480, and the distribution is strongly right-skewed because a handful of corporate contracts pay thousands. Reading one — the mean — suggests the typical student pays GH₵742 per term. It is arithmetically correct and practically wrong: no student pays that amount; the number is pulled upward by 11 corporate contracts. Reading two — the median — says the typical student pays GH₵480, which is the most useful single sentence for a pricing decision: half the students pay less than that, half more. Reading three — the percentiles — says p10 = GH₵150, p25 = GH₵300, p75 = GH₵650, p95 = GH₵2,300. Now the centre and the spread are visible, and the conversation changes: the bottom quarter of students are paying less than two-thirds of the median, which is exactly the group a hardship policy would target. The same table, three sentences: a mean that misleads, a median that informs, and percentiles that decide. Notice that no statistics beyond arithmetic were needed — only the discipline to look at the shape before quoting a number.
describing-and-visualising-data.challenge: Produce a one-page analytical note on a question from your own work or study: a headline sentence, a distribution described with count, centre, spread and tail, one chart that makes the claim checkable, one honest caveat about the data, and a recommendation. Give it to somebody who does not know the data and ask them to state your conclusion and one thing they would need to verify before acting on it.

from-analysis-to-decision.title: Welcome to From analysis to decisions, part of Data Science & Analytics.
from-analysis-to-decision.idea: Most analysts can produce a number. Fewer can produce a decision. The gap is made of three things: getting the data at the level of detail the decision needs, presenting it so that it can be understood in ten seconds, and — where a choice must be made between two options — running a test that gives a defensible answer instead of a hopeful one.
from-analysis-to-decision.example: The question: does a WhatsApp reminder the evening before a session increase attendance? The centre has six weeks and 20 sessions a week of data to work with. Design first: the primary metric is attendance rate per student per session (attendances ÷ invitations), the baseline is 61%, the minimum effect worth acting on is 5 percentage points, and the test runs for four weeks. Students are randomised within each session so that time of day and instructor cannot explain the difference, and nobody is told which group they were allocated to. The result is a rate in each group, the absolute difference and its confidence interval. Note what the numbers license you to say and what they do not: "reminders raised attendance by about 6 points, and the plausible range is 2 to 10 points" supports a decision to send them every week. It does not support the claim that reminders cause long-term retention, which is a different question with a longer horizon. The last step is the one most teams skip: the recommendation is written with its owner, the cost (one part-time staff member's hour a day), the expected effect, and the date on which somebody will check whether the effect persisted after the novelty wore off.
from-analysis-to-decision.challenge: Run one real experiment from question to decision, even a small one: define the metric and the minimum effect, randomise where you can, collect enough data for the analysis to mean something, compute the difference with a confidence interval, and write the five-sentence handover with an owner and a check-back date. Then do the check-back, and report whether the effect persisted — including if it did not.
